newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition stays together, but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: German coalition stays together, but doubts remain.

text.p: Germany's fragile coalition pledged on Monday to stick together, but a festering dispute over tax increases to fill deficit holes and qualify for Europe's single currency cast doubts over the government's future.

As reports surfaced that Chancellor Helmut Kohl had threatened to resign over the budget impasse, leaders of his centre-right coalition said the 14-year-old alliance between the Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) would survive.

Erwin Teufel, a CDU leader and state premier of Baden- Wuerttemberg, said he expected the coalition would weather the current storm, but added there was nevertheless a possibility it could collapse because of the budget dispute.
"The situation reminds me of 1966," said Teufel before a meeting of CDU leaders in Bonn, referring to the last time a coalition made up of Christian Democrats and liberals broke up.
"No one wanted the coalition to end then either, but it just happened," he said.
The Hamburger Morgenpost newspaper said on Monday that Kohl had threatened to resign on four occasions last week over the budget row. But a chancellery spokesman denied the report.

The newspaper quoted coalition sources saying that Kohl had offered to quit during two crisis meetings held in his chancellery last Sunday and Tuesday. Last November Kohl threatened to resign amid a row over the 1997 budget.

But commentators said they believed it had been an empty threat that Kohl was easily talked out of because leaders of both the CDU and FDP realise there are few palatable alternatives to remaining in the coalition.

Wolfgang Gerhardt, the FDP chairman, told journalists in Bonn on Monday the differences were narrowing between his party and Kohl's CDU on new budget savings measures without tax increases in 1997 and 1998.
"The coalition will stick together," said Gerhardt.

But the Hamburger Morgenpost newspaper reported that Waigel had met former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt to discuss the possible formation of a grand coalition between the Social Democrats (SPD) and the CDU/CSU if the current governing alliance breaks apart.
Schmidt's office confirmed the meeting. But SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine dismissed the talk of a grand coalition.
"A grand coalition is out of the question," Lafontaine said. "If this government doesn't know where it is going, then there must be new elections."
Schmidt, in a separate television interview on Monday, called on Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel to resign over what he said was the government's fiscal mismanagement.
Worries about deficits and monetary union sent German share prices sharply lower after a strong start. The blue chip DAX index fell 70 points off its highs to a close of 3,667 points.

Serious disagreements over the gaping holes for both the 1997 and 1998 budgets have torn at the threads of the coalition for months. The FDP has firmly opposed any tax increases while Waigel refuses to rule out raising some taxes in 1998.

The failure to close the budget holes has reduced the chances that Germany will meet fiscal requirements for European economic and monetary union. The Maastricht Treaty permits budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
The deficits and prospects Germany will not be eligible for the euro opened the door to a heated debate on the common currency that had long been stifled by a broad consensus among political elites.
Some leaders have now proposed taking a more relaxed view on the Maastricht criteria while others have argued for delaying EMU.

Kohl warned of dire consequences if the euro were delayed. Speaking in Dresden, he said critics who say the single currency should be postponed should consider the effects this would have on the German mark and on German exports.
But Bavaria state Premier Edmund Stoiber, a prominent figure in the CDU's sister party Christian Social Union, said that meeting the Maastricht criteria was more important than the timetable.
Economics Minister Gunter Rexrodt, a member of the liberal Free Democrats, said monetary union should not be delayed because it would be economically damaging and politically shortsighted.
"I see the current delay debate as dangerous in economic and political terms," he said. "Credibility and reliability as well as the political will to grow together would be damaged."
